query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a lanthanum dopant into boride‐based alloys will enhance their resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion by promoting in situ formation of a stable, protective oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that demonstrate measurable molten-aluminum corrosion at around 660°C.
generation.intervention: A single-step composition modification by adding a controlled amount of lanthanum into the boride-based material during synthesis.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at approximately 660°C under typical hot-dip plating operational conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Lanthanum segregates at the alloy grain boundaries and interfaces to catalyze the formation of a protective oxide (e.g., La2O3) on the component surface.
generation.mechanism: The doped lanthanum modifies the intrinsic chemistry of the boride-based alloy so that during high-temperature exposure, a stable and adherent oxide barrier forms. This barrier slows down the diffusion and reaction of aluminum with the base material, thereby reducing corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Lanthanum-doped boride-based components should exhibit a significantly lower corrosion rate—quantifiable via reduced mass loss and lower corrosion current densities—compared to untreated components under identical hot-dip aluminum plating conditions.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components with the conventional composition (i.e., without lanthanum dopant).
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected to hold when the lanthanum concentration is optimized to form a continuous protective oxide without promoting unwanted secondary phases, and when operating within the temperature and chemical environment typical of hot-dip aluminum-plating (≈660°C molten aluminum).
generation.uncertainty: The optimal lanthanum dosage and the precise magnitude of corrosion rate reduction remain to be quantified; the long-term stability of the doped oxide layer under cyclical thermal stresses also requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of boride-based samples: one group with the optimized lanthanum dopant and a control group with the standard composition. Subject both groups to molten aluminum immersion at 660°C under conditions that mimic hot-dip aluminum plating. Measure corrosion performance over time.
measurements: Electrochemical corrosion current density via potentiodynamic polarization
Surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM/EDS) for oxide layer characterization
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the lanthanum-doped samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., at least a 30% reduction in corrosion rate or comparable improvement in oxide stability) over the control under identical conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. AbstractSurface condition and corrosion resistance are major concerns when metallic materials are going to be utilized for applications. In this study, FeCoNiCr medium-entropy alloy (MEA) is first treated with a nitrogen atmospheric-pressure plasma jet (APPJ) and then coated with octadecyltrichlorosilane (OTS) for the surface modification. The hydrophobicity of the FeCoNiCr MEA was effectively improved by OTS-coating treatment, APPJ treatment, or the combination of both treatments (OTS-coated APPJ-treated), which increased the water contact angle from 54.49° of the bare MEA to 70.56°, 93.94°, and 88.42°, respectively. Potentiodynamic polarization and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy tests demonstrate that the APPJ-treated FeCoNiCr MEA exhibits the best anti-corrosion properties. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy reveals that APPJ treatment at 700 °C oxidizes all the alloying elements in the FeCoNiCr MEA, which demonstrates that a short APPJ treatment of two-minute is effective in forming a metal oxide layer on the surface to improve the corrosion resistance of FeCoNiCr MEA. These results provide a convenient and rapid method for improving surface properties of FeCoNiCr MEA.Key

frame.system: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment that are exposed directly to molten aluminum during processing.
frame.goal: To improve the components' resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion via a single intervention.
frame.limitation: Current boride-based materials are susceptible to degradation (corrosion) when in contact with molten aluminum under plating conditions.
constraints: The intervention must be singular (i.e., a one-step modification or treatment).
Performance improvement must be quantifiable relative to a baseline (current corrosion rate of untreated boride-based components).
The intervention must remain effective under the high-temperature, chemically aggressive conditions of molten aluminum.
frame.regime: High-temperature molten aluminum environment (approximately 660°C) characteristic of hot-dip aluminum plating, where chemical and thermal stresses are significant.
prior_attempts: Previous strategies have included alloying modifications and applying multi-layered coatings, yet these have either been too complex or have not demonstrated clear improvements in corrosion resistance under the aggressive conditions.
Thin protective coatings or surface treatments have been explored but not definitively optimized as a single intervention for boride-based surfaces.

decision.trend: Early work to address corrosion in harsh environments mainly relied on surface modification techniques such as plasma treatments and organic coatings to form protective oxide layers, as seen in PMC7240591. Although these surface or interface engineering approaches improved the immediate corrosion resistance under aggressive conditions, they did not fully overcome the inherent chemical limitations of the base metals. More recently, research in related high‐performance alloys has shown that a shift toward modifying the bulk composition (i.e., a dopant addition) can lead to in situ formation of more stable, adherent oxide films that endure high-temperature exposure. This progression—from external coatings to an integrated alloy composition change—demonstrates an emerging trend wherein adjusting the intrinsic chemistry leads to a more robust barrier against corrosive molten media.
decision.unsolved: For boride-based components in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, the central unsolved issue remains: how to achieve a single-step, compositionally integrated intervention that consistently forms and maintains a protective surface barrier against molten aluminum attack at around 660°C. Existing strategies either require multi-layered treatments or do not adequately address the long-term stability of the protective phase under high-temperature chemical stresses.
decision.why: Following the observed trend—from external surface modifications to controlled dopant strategies—the most plausible next step is to modify the boride-based material by adding a lanthanum dopant. Lanthanum is known to segregate at critical interfaces and promote the formation of a stable, protective oxide layer that can inhibit aluminum dissolution. This approach, which fits within the niche of a single, material/process intervention, directly addresses the molten-aluminum corrosion challenge under hot-dip plating conditions and builds on prior evidence that alloy composition adjustments can enhance corrosion resistance.
